credit: The use-it-twice bug (add, never overwrite) follows Andrej Karpathy's micrograd video, 'The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation'.

chapters.name: A million nudges
chapters.note: nudge one weight, rerun everything, repeat forever

cap.1: To learn, a model needs to know how each of its millions of numbers affected the result. Nudging them one at a time would take millions of runs.
cap.2: Finite differences needs a forward pass per parameter: fine as a sanity check, hopeless for training. Backprop gets every gradient from one forward and one backward pass.
cap.3: Numerical differentiation costs one forward pass per parameter. Reverse-mode AD gets all gradients of one scalar in a single backward sweep, provided the forward pass kept a record.

cap.1: Picture a kitchen where every bowl gets a card taped on: which recipe made it, and which bowls went in. Shop-bought ingredients have no card.
cap.2: That is the computational graph. Each tensor made by an operation carries a recipe: the function, its arguments and its parent tensors. Leaves like weights have none.
cap.3: Each non-leaf tensor stores a recipe (func, args, kwargs, parents by argument position). Together the recipes form a DAG from the leaves up to the loss, built as the forward pass runs.

cap.1: Run the forward pass and the cards appear as you go. Each arrow says 'this was made from that'. Nothing is worked out backwards yet; it is only remembered.
cap.2: wrap_forward_fn wraps a plain numpy function so its output Tensor comes with a recipe attached. The graph is built as the code runs, one card per operation.
cap.3: wrap_forward_fn lifts numpy ops generically: unwrap Tensor args, compute, wrap the output, attach Recipe(func, args, kwargs, parents). The DAG is whatever this run executed.

cap.1: When the dish tastes wrong, follow the cards backwards to share out the blame. Bowl b went into two things, so it collects blame from both.
cap.2: The backward pass walks the recorded graph from L to the leaves. Each recipe's backward function splits the incoming gradient among its parents. b gets two pieces, which add.
cap.3: dL/db = ∂L/∂c · ∂c/∂b + ∂L/∂b = a + 1, one term per outgoing edge. Walk in topological order so each node's incoming gradient is complete before its backward runs.

chapters.name: Overwrite, not add
chapters.verdict: A bowl used twice collects blame twice. Add, never overwrite.

cap.1: If each new share of blame replaces the last instead of adding to it, a bowl used twice gets only part of its blame. Nothing crashes. It is just wrong.
cap.2: Assigning instead of accumulating keeps one path's gradient. For x*x you get x instead of 2x. It looks plausible, so training still seems to work.
cap.3: Fan-out requires accumulation: grads[node] = grads.get(node, 0) + contribution. Overwriting returns one term of the sum. Test d(x·x)/dx = 2x, then check against central differences.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: loss.backward() walks this graph for you
Weights are leaves: their blame lands in .grad
Attribution walks the same graph from output to insides

cap.1: Every time you call loss.backward(), this recorded graph is the map it follows. Knowing it is there explains most autograd surprises.
cap.2: Only what was recorded can get a gradient. Leaves such as weights get theirs written to .grad; intermediate tensors only hold theirs temporarily during the walk.
cap.3: Gradient-based attribution in interpretability runs this same backward walk from an output to inner activations, so what the graph records bounds what those attributions can mean.

coda.title: L = a·b + b uses b twice. Find b's blame.

caption.1: Drag a and b. The blue line's slope is b's total blame and always matches the nudge check. The pink line counts one path only and is off by exactly 1.
caption.2: b feeds both the product and the sum, so its gradient is the sum of two pieces, a + 1. The nudge check agrees; the one-path slope never does.
caption.3: Fan-out sums: dL/db = ∂(ab)/∂b + ∂b/∂b = a + 1, confirmed by central differences. Dropping either term is the overwrite bug.

where_else: loss.backward() in every PyTorch training loop
Spreadsheets tracking which cells depend on which, so they recalculate in the right order
Build tools like make, which record what each file was built from
Gradient-based attribution in interpretability, walking back from an output to inner activations

hamming.what: A record, made during the forward pass, of which operation produced each tensor and from which parents.
hamming.when: Every time you compute from tensors that need gradients, which is every training step.
hamming.why: Backprop needs a route from the loss back to every weight, and recording it as you go gets every gradient in one backward sweep instead of one run per weight.

object.title: The recipe tree
object.subtitle: Balls are tensors, rods say 'made from'; the loss sits on top, the leaves at the bottom.

cap.1: Each ball is a tensor and each rod says 'made from'. The loss sits on top; the things it was made from sit below.
cap.2: The forward pass built this: every operation recorded its parents. L is the root; W and x are leaves.
cap.3: A DAG of recipes: nodes are tensors, edges run parent to child. ARENA calls L the root and the parameters leaves, because backprop starts at L.

cap.1: The forward pass climbs upwards, leaving a card at every stop. Nothing is differentiated yet; it is only remembered.
cap.2: Recording is cheap bookkeeping during the forward pass. The gradients come later, from walking these rods back down.
cap.3: The graph is dynamic: it records exactly the operations this run executed, so control flow in Python shapes the DAG.

cap.1: x feeds two places: the product with W and the shortcut. Two rods leave it, so two shares of blame come back and add up.
cap.2: Fan-out: x has two consumers, so dL/dx is the sum of the gradient through a and the gradient straight from r.
cap.3: The residual r = x + f(x) is the canonical fan-out: dL/dx = dL/dr + J_fᵀ·dL/dr. Overwriting instead of accumulating drops one of the two terms.

cap.1: Backward walks down from L. Each ball waits until everything above it has passed its share down.
cap.2: Topological order guarantees every consumer of a node has contributed before that node's backward runs.
cap.3: Reverse topological traversal from the root makes each node's accumulated grad_out complete before its backward function fires.

cap.1: W is a leaf you can change. Its blame lands in W.grad, ready for the optimiser to use.
cap.2: Leaves get their gradients written to .grad; intermediates like h and a only hold theirs during the walk.
cap.3: is_leaf and requires_grad decide whether a gradient is written to .grad or held in temporary storage and discarded.

predict.q: x feeds both the product and the shortcut. What is its gradient?

options.t: The sum of the pieces from both paths
Whichever path the walk reached last

predict.why: Each outgoing rod sends back a share, and dL/dx is their sum. Keeping only one is the overwrite bug.

predict.q: Why does the forward pass record anything at all?

options.t: So the backward pass has a route: which op made each tensor, from which parents
To make the forward pass faster

predict.why: Without the recorded recipes there is nothing to walk backwards along.

predict.q: Where does W's gradient end up?

options.t: In W.grad, because W is a leaf

predict.why: Leaves get their gradients written to .grad; intermediate tensors only hold theirs temporarily.

object.where: Any dependency record you can walk backwards: spreadsheets, build tools, provenance logs, autograd.
